Non-homogeneous boundary value problems for coupled KdV-KdV systems posed on the half line

Shenghao Li, Min Chen, Xin Yang and Bing-Yu Zhang
Abstract

In this article, we study an initial-boundary-value problem of a coupled KdV-KdV system on the half line ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+} with non-homogeneous boundary conditions:

{ut+vx+u​ux+vx​x​x=0,vt+ux+(v​u)x+ux​x​x=0,u(x,0)=ϕ(x),v(x,0)=ψ(x),u(0,t)=h1(t),v(0,t)=h2(t),vx(0,t)=h3(t),x,t>0.\begin{cases}u_{t}+v_{x}+uu_{x}+v_{xxx}=0,\\ v_{t}+u_{x}+(vu)_{x}+u_{xxx}=0,\\ u(x,0)=\phi(x),\quad v(x,0)=\psi(x),\\ u(0,t)=h_{1}(t),\quad v(0,t)=h_{2}(t),\quad v_{x}(0,t)=h_{3}(t),\end{cases}\qquad x,\,t>0.

It is shown that the problem is locally unconditionally well-posed in Hs​(ℝ+)×Hs​(ℝ+)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) for s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} with initial data (ϕ,ψ)(\phi,\psi) in Hs​(ℝ+)×Hs​(ℝ+)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and boundary data (h1,h2,h3)(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3}) in Hs+13​(ℝ+)×Hs+13​(ℝ+)×Hs3​(ℝ+)H^{\frac{s+1}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{\frac{s+1}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{\frac{s}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+}). The approach developed in this paper can also be applied to study more general KdV-KdV systems posed on the half line.

1 Introduction

The coupled KdV-KdV system

{ut+vx+u​ux+vx​x​x=0,vt+ux+(v​u)x+ux​x​x=0,\begin{cases}u_{t}+v_{x}+uu_{x}+v_{xxx}=0,\\ v_{t}+u_{x}+(vu)_{x}+u_{xxx}=0,\end{cases} (1.1)

is a special case of a broad class of Boussinesq systems or the so-called abcd systems derived by Bona, Chen and Saut in [BCS02, BCS04] from the two-dimensional Euler equations. Compared to those uni-directional models, such as the KdV equation, the Boussinesq equation and the BBM equation, the bi-directional systems (1.1) provide wider range of applications in reality. The Cauchy problem of the system (1.1) posed either on ℝ\mathbb{R} or on the periodic domain 𝕋\mathbb{T} has been well studied. In particular, it is known to be analytically well-posed in the space Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4}, but related bilinear estimates fail in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any s<−34s<-\frac{3}{4}. (See e.g. [AC08, BGK10, YZ22a]). In this paper, we are concerned with the well-posedness of the initial-boundary-value problem (IBVP) for the coupled KdV-KdV system posed on the half line ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+}:

{ut+vx+u​ux+vx​x​x=0,vt+ux+(v​u)x+ux​x​x=0,u(x,0)=ϕ(x),v(x,0)=ψ(x),u(0,t)=h1(t),v(0,t)=h2(t),vx(0,t)=h3(t).x,t>0.\begin{cases}u_{t}+v_{x}+uu_{x}+v_{xxx}=0,\\ v_{t}+u_{x}+(vu)_{x}+u_{xxx}=0,\\ u(x,0)=\phi(x),\quad v(x,0)=\psi(x),\\ u(0,t)=h_{1}(t),\quad v(0,t)=h_{2}(t),\quad v_{x}(0,t)=h_{3}(t).\end{cases}\qquad x,\,t>0. (1.2)

Let’s first briefly review some highly related literatures. The IBVP for the single KdV equation

{wt+wx+wx​x​x=0,w(x,0)=ϕ(x),w(0,t)=h(t).x,t>0.\begin{cases}w_{t}+w_{x}+w_{xxx}=0,\\ w(x,0)=\phi(x),\quad w(0,t)=h(t).\end{cases}\qquad x,\,t>0. (1.3)

posed on the half line has been investigated extensively. Bona, Sun and Zhang[BSZ02] developed a method by using the Laplace transform to establish the well-posedness of (1.3) in the space Hs​(ℝ+)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) for s>34s>\frac{3}{4}. Later, they improved the range of ss to be s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} in [BSZ06] by taking advantage of the Fourier restriction spaces introduced by Bourgain[Bou93a]. During the same period, Colliander and Kenig[CK02] introduced the Duhamel boundary forcing operator to establish the well-posedness of (1.3) in the space Hs​(ℝ+)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) for s≥0s\geq 0. After that, Holmer[Hol06] generalized this method to improve the range of the index ss to be s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} by constructing an analytic family of boundary forcing operators. These two methods automatically establish locally analytical well-posedness since both of them took advantage of a certain fixed point argument. As a result, the threshold −34-\frac{3}{4} is optimal concerning the analytical well-posedness, see [CCT03]. These two methods were also applied to study the well-posedness of the IBVP for more general equations, such as the Boussinesq equations [Xue08, CT17, LCZ18], the BBM equation [BCH14], the nonlinear Schodinger equations [Hol05, ET16, Cav17, BSZ18, GW20], the Klein-Gordon-Schodinger system [CT19], the Schodinger-KdV systems [CC19] and many more. But few works have been devoted to investigate the low regularity well-posedness of the IBVP for KdV-KdV systems such as (1.2). Part of the reason is due to the complicated structure of the systems. Actually, it was discovered in [Oh09] and [YZ22a] that the threshold index for the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for KdV-KdV systems on ℝ\mathbb{R} may be as large as 00 or 34\frac{3}{4} instead of −34-\frac{3}{4}, depending on the dispersion coefficients and how uu and vv are interacted in the systems. The goal of this paper is to study the IBVP for the particular KdV-KdV system (1.2) on the half line ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+} and establish the well-posedness beyond the threshold −34-\frac{3}{4}.

In order to adopt results and techniques obtained in the study of KdV-type equations, the new variables U:=14​(u+v)U:=\frac{1}{4}(u+v) and V:=14​(u−v)V:=\frac{1}{4}(u-v) are introduced so that the linear parts of (1.2) on UU and VV are decoupled with the KdV type. More precisely, the new system reads as

{Ut+Ux+Ux​x​x+3​U​Ux+(U​V)x−V​Vx=0,Vt−Vx−Vx​x​x−U​Ux+(U​V)x+3​V​Vx=0,U(x,0)=14(ϕ+ψ),V(x,0)=14(ϕ−ψ),U(0,t)=14(h1+h2),V(0,t)=14(h1−h2),Vx(0,t)−Ux(0,t)=−12h3.x,t>0.\begin{cases}U_{t}+U_{x}+U_{xxx}+3UU_{x}+(UV)_{x}-VV_{x}=0,\vskip 2.168pt\\ V_{t}-V_{x}-V_{xxx}-UU_{x}+(UV)_{x}+3VV_{x}=0,\vskip 2.168pt\\ U(x,0)=\frac{1}{4}(\phi+\psi),\quad V(x,0)=\frac{1}{4}(\phi-\psi),\vskip 2.168pt\\ U(0,t)=\frac{1}{4}(h_{1}+h_{2}),\quad V(0,t)=\frac{1}{4}(h_{1}-h_{2}),\quad V_{x}(0,t)-U_{x}(0,t)=-\frac{1}{2}h_{3}.\end{cases}\qquad x,\,t>0.

For ease of notations, we still denote (U,V)(U,V) as (u,v)(u,v), and write (14​(ϕ+ψ),14​(ϕ−ψ))\left(\frac{1}{4}(\phi+\psi),\frac{1}{4}(\phi-\psi)\right) as (ϕ,ψ)(\phi,\psi) and (14​(h1+h2),14​(h1−h2),−12​h3)\left(\frac{1}{4}(h_{1}+h_{2}),\frac{1}{4}(h_{1}-h_{2}),-\frac{1}{2}h_{3}\right) as (h1,h2,h3)(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3}). Then it reduces to study the following IBVP:

{ut+ux​x​x+ux+3​u​ux+(u​v)x−v​vx=0,vt−vx​x​x−vx−u​ux+(u​v)x+3​v​vx=0,u(x,0)=ϕ(x),v(x,0)=ψ(x),u(0,t)=h1(t),v(0,t)=h2(t),vx(0,t)−ux(0,t)=h3(t),x,t>0.\begin{cases}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+u_{x}+3uu_{x}+(uv)_{x}-vv_{x}=0,\\ v_{t}-v_{xxx}-v_{x}-uu_{x}+(uv)_{x}+3vv_{x}=0,\\ u(x,0)=\phi(x),\quad v(x,0)=\psi(x),\\ u(0,t)=h_{1}(t),\quad v(0,t)=h_{2}(t),\quad v_{x}(0,t)-u_{x}(0,t)=h_{3}(t),\end{cases}\qquad x,t>0. (1.4)

which is equivalent to the IBVP (1.2) for the well-posedness in the space Hs​(ℝ+)×Hs​(ℝ+)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}).

For any s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, we define

ℋxs​(ℝ+):=Hs​(ℝ+)×Hs​(ℝ+),ℋts​(ℝ+):=Hs+13​(ℝ+)×Hs+13​(ℝ+)×Hs3​(ℝ+).{\cal H}_{x}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}):=H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}),\quad{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+}):=H^{\frac{s+1}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{\frac{s+1}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{\frac{s}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+}).

When s≥3s\geq 3, the well-posedness of (1.4) in the space Hs​(ℝ+)×Hs​(ℝ+)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) can be established concerning the classical solutions (u,v)∈C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))(u,v)\in C([0,T];{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})). So in the remaining of this paper, we will focus on the case s≤3s\leq 3. In addition, for lower regularity solutions, there will be a serious uniqueness issue. For more details, the readers can refer to Remark 2.4 in section 2. In this situation, the type of solutions of (1.4) that we are interested in is the so-called mild solutions which can be viewed as limits of strong solutions. The precise definition is given below.

Definition 1.1 (Mild solutions).

Let s≤3s\leq 3 and T>0T>0 be given.

  • (i)

    A function pair (u,v)∈C⁡([0,T],ℋx3​(ℝ+))∩C1​([0,T],ℋx0​(ℝ+))(u,v)\in C([0,T];{\cal H}^{3}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+}))\cap C^{1}([0,T];{\cal H}^{0}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})) is said to be a strong solution of the IBVP (1.4) in the space C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))C([0,T];{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})) if the equations in (1.4) hold for a.e. (x,t)∈ℝ+×(0,T)(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\times(0,T) and (u,v,vx)|x=0∈ℋts​(0,T)(u,v,v_{x})|_{x=0}\in{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(0,T).

  • (ii)

    A function pair (u,v)∈C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))(u,v)\in C([0,T];{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})) is said to be a mild solution of the IBVP (1.4) if there exists a sequence of strong solutions (un,vn)∈C⁡([0,T],ℋx3​(ℝ+))(u_{n},v_{n})\in C([0,T];{\cal H}^{3}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})) such that limn→∞(un,vn)→(u,v)\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}(u_{n},v_{n})\to(u,v) in C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))C([0,T];{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})) and limn→0(h1,n,h2,n,h3,n)→(h1,h2,h3)\lim\limits_{n\to 0}(h_{1,n},h_{2,n},h_{3,n})\to(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3}) in ℋts​(0,T){\cal H}^{s}_{t}(0,T), where (h1,n,h2,n,h3,n):=(un,vn,∂xvn)|x=0(h_{1,n},h_{2,n},h_{3,n}):=\left.(u_{n},v_{n},\partial_{x}v_{n})\right|_{x=0}.

After the concept of solutions is fixed, we can discuss the (unconditional) local well-posedness of (1.4) which is understood in the following sense.

Definition 1.2 (Local well-posedness).

For any s≤3s\leq 3, the IBVP (1.4) is said to be locally well-posed in the space ℋxs​(ℝ+){\cal H}_{x}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) if for any r>0r>0, there exists some time T>0T>0, depending only on rr and ss, such that for any naturally compatible 11 1 For the concept of compatibility, the reader can refer to Definition 2.7. (ϕ,ψ)∈ℋxs​(ℝ+)(\phi,\psi)\in{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and h→=(h1,h2,h3)∈ℋts​(ℝ+)\vec{h}=(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})\in{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) with ∥ϕ,ψ)∥ℋxs​(ℝ+)+∥h→∥ℋts​(ℝ+)≤r\|\phi,\psi)\|_{{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}+\|\vec{h}\|_{{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\leq r, the IBVP (1.4) admits a unique mild solution (u,v)∈C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))(u,v)\in C([0,T];{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})) and, moreover, the solution map is continuous in the corresponding spaces. If the solution map is real analytic instead, then the IBVP (1.4) is said to be locally analytically well-posed.

We intend to find those values of ss for which the IBVP (1.4) is locally well-posed in the space ℋxs​(ℝ+){\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+}). The following theorem is the main result of this paper.

Theorem 1.3.

The IBVP (1.4) is locally analytically well-posed in the space ℋxs​(ℝ+){\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+}), with any naturally compatible data (ϕ,ψ)∈ℋxs​(ℝ+)(\phi,\psi)\in{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and h→=(h1,h2,h3)∈ℋts​(ℝ+)\vec{h}=(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})\in{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+}), for any s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4}.

To prove Theorem 1.3 which is a result on local well-posedness, we use scaling argument to introduce

where β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1] is a parameter. Then (1.4) becomes

where

When s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4},

‖(ϕβ,ψβ)‖ℋxs​(ℝ+)≲β38​‖(ϕ,ψ)‖ℋ1s​(ℝ+),‖(h1β,h2β,h3β)‖ℋts​(ℝ+)≲β38​‖(h1,h2,h3)‖ℋts​(ℝ+),\|(\phi^{\beta},\psi^{\beta})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\lesssim\beta^{\frac{3}{8}}\|(\phi,\psi)\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}_{1}(\mathbb{R}^{+})},\quad\|(h_{1}^{\beta},h_{2}^{\beta},h_{3}^{\beta})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\lesssim\beta^{\frac{3}{8}}\|(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+})},

which implies

Thus, in order to prove Theorem 1.3, it is sufficient to establish Theorem 1.4 below for the following IBVP:

{ut+ux​x​x+β​ux+3​u​ux+(u​v)x−v​vx=0,vt−vx​x​x−β​vx−u​ux+(u​v)x+3​v​vx=0,u(x,0)=ϕ(x),v(x,0)=ψ(x),u(0,t)=h1(t),v(0,t)=h2(t),vx(0,t)−ux(0,t)=h3(t).x,t>0.\begin{cases}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+\beta u_{x}+3uu_{x}+(uv)_{x}-vv_{x}=0,\\ v_{t}-v_{xxx}-\beta v_{x}-uu_{x}+(uv)_{x}+3vv_{x}=0,\\ u(x,0)=\phi(x),\quad v(x,0)=\psi(x),\\ u(0,t)=h_{1}(t),\quad v(0,t)=h_{2}(t),\quad v_{x}(0,t)-u_{x}(0,t)=h_{3}(t).\end{cases}\qquad x,t>0. (1.5)
Theorem 1.4.

For any s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} and T>0T>0, there exists an ϵ>0\epsilon>0, depending only on TT and ss, such that for any β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1] and for any naturally compatible data (ϕ,ψ)∈ℋxs​(ℝ+)(\phi,\psi)\in{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and h→=(h1,h2,h3)∈ℋts​(ℝ+)\vec{h}=(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})\in{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) with

∥ϕ,ψ)∥ℋxs​(ℝ+)+∥h→∥ℋts​(ℝ+)≤ϵ,\|\phi,\psi)\|_{{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}+\|\vec{h}\|_{{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\leq\epsilon,

the IBVP (1.5) admits a unique mild solution (u,v)∈C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))(u,v)\in C\big([0,T];{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\big), and moreover, the solution map is real analytic in the corresponding spaces.

We remark that the well-posedness obtained in Theorem 1.4 (or equivalently Theorem 1.3) is unconditional (see Remark 2.4) since the uniqueness is secured in the space C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))C\big([0,T];{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\big) itself rather than in a smaller subspace. The reason that the unconditional uniqueness can be justified is because we are concerning with the mild solutions. If the distributional solutions, instead of the mild solutions, are adopted in Definition 1.2, then the unconditional uniqueness is still a challenging open problem.

2 Outline of the method and applications

2.1 Key ingredients in the proof of Theorem 1.4

Theorem 1.4 will be proved using the approach similar to that developed in [BSZ02, BSZ06, CK02, Hol06] for the KdV equation but with some modifications to handle the bi-directional system (1.5). Consider the Cauchy problem for the linear KdV-type equation posed on ℝ\mathbb{R},

wt+α​wx​x​x+β​wx=0,w⁡(x,0)=w0​(x),x∈ℝ,t∈ℝ,w_{t}+\alpha w_{xxx}+\beta w_{x}=0,\qquad w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},\,t\in\mathbb{R}, (2.1)

where α∈ℝ\{0}\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\backslash\{0\} and β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R}. Let WRα,βW_{R}^{\alpha,\beta} be the semigroup operator associated to (2.1). The solution of (2.1) is then given explicitly by

WRα,β​(t)​w0​(x)=∫ℝei​ξ​x​ei​ϕα,β​(ξ)​t​w0^​(ξ)​𝑑ξ,W_{R}^{\alpha,\beta}(t)w_{0}(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\xi x}e^{i\phi^{\alpha,\beta}(\xi)t}\widehat{w_{0}}(\xi)d\xi, (2.2)

where w0^​(ξ)\widehat{w_{0}}(\xi) is the Fourier transform of w0​(x)w_{0}(x), and ϕα,β\phi^{\alpha,\beta} is the cubic polynomial defined as below:

ϕα,β​(ξ)=α​ξ3−β​ξ.\phi^{\alpha,\beta}(\xi)=\alpha\xi^{3}-\beta\xi. (2.3)
Definition 2.1.

For α,β,s,b∈ℝ\alpha,\beta,s,b\in\mathbb{R}, the Fourier restriction space Xs,bα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b} is defined to be the completion of the Schwarz class 𝒮⁡(ℝ2){\mathcal{S}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) under the norm

‖w‖Xs,bα,β=‖⟨ξ⟩s​⟨τ−ϕα,β​(ξ)⟩b​w^​(ξ,τ)‖Lξ,τ2​(ℝ2),\|w\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b}}=\left\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\phi^{\alpha,\beta}(\xi)\rangle^{b}\widehat{w}(\xi,\tau)\right\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}, (2.4)

where ϕα,β\phi^{\alpha,\beta} is as defined in (2.3) and w^\widehat{w} represents the space-time Fourier transform of ww.

When b>12b>\frac{1}{2}, it follows directly from the Sobolev embedding that Xs,bα,β⊂Ct​(ℝ,Hs​(ℝ))X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b}\subset C_{t}(\mathbb{R};H^{s}(\mathbb{R})). But the estimate on the boundary integral operator (see e.g. Lemma 4.3 and 4.10) forces b≤12b\leq\frac{1}{2}, and then the space Xs,bα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b} may not be in Ct​(ℝ,Hs​(ℝ))C_{t}(\mathbb{R};H^{s}(\mathbb{R})). In addition, the bilinear estimates used in the Cauchy problems will fail. In order to overcome these difficulties, we introduce some modified Fourier restriction spaces Xs,b,σα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b,\sigma} and Ys,b,σα,βY_{s,b,\sigma}^{\alpha,\beta}. The spaces Xs,b,σα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b,\sigma} will be used to justify the bilinear estimates and Ys,b,σα,βY_{s,b,\sigma}^{\alpha,\beta} will serve as suitable solution spaces.

Definition 2.2.

For α,β,s,b∈ℝ\alpha,\beta,s,b\in\mathbb{R} and σ>12\sigma>\frac{1}{2}, let Λs,σα,β\Lambda^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma} be the completion of the Schwarz class 𝒮⁡(ℝ2){\mathcal{S}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) under the norm

We will first establish the following conditional well-posedness.

Theorem 2.3 (Conditional Well-posedness).

Let −34<s≤3-\frac{3}{4}<s\leq 3, T>0T>0 and 0≤β≤10\leq\beta\leq 1 be given. There exist σ=σ⁡(s)>12\sigma=\sigma(s)>\frac{1}{2} and r=r⁡(s,T)>0r=r(s,T)>0 such that for any naturally compatible (ϕ,ψ)∈ℋxs​(ℝ+)(\phi,\psi)\in{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+}), h→=(h1,h2,h3)∈ℋts​(ℝ+)\vec{h}=(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})\in{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) related to the IBVP (1.5) with

∥ϕ,ψ)∥ℋxs​(ℝ+)+∥h→∥ℋts​(ℝ+)≤r,\|\phi,\psi)\|_{{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}+\|\vec{h}\|_{{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\leq r,

the system of the integral equations (SIE) (2.11) admits a unique solution

(u,v)∈𝒴σ​(ΩT):=Ys,12,σ1,β​(ΩT)×Ys,12,σ−1,−β​(ΩT)(u,v)\in\mathcal{Y}_{\sigma}(\Omega_{T}):=Y^{1,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}(\Omega_{T})\times Y^{-1,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}(\Omega_{T})

Moreover, the solution map is real analytic in the corresponding spaces.

Remark 2.4.

The well-posedness presented in Theorem 2.3 is conditional in the sense that the solution (u,v)∈C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))(u,v)\in C([0,T];\mathcal{H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})) of (2.11) is in fact the restriction for a function defined on ℝ×ℝ\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R} to the region (0,T)×ℝ+(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{+}, and the uniqueness of the solution holds in a subspace 𝒴σ​(ΩT)\mathcal{Y}_{\sigma}(\Omega_{T}) rather than in the full space C⁡([0,T],ℋxs​(ℝ+))C([0,T];\mathcal{H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})), which leads to a serious issue: If a solution of the IBVP (1.5) is found in a different approach, will it be the same as that presented by Theorem 2.3?

In this paper, we will prove Theorem 1.4 to give a positive answer to the above question. The justification of Theorem 1.4 follows from Theorem 2.3 and the following two further properties.

  • (i)

    the solution of SIE (2.11) is a mild solution of the IBVP (1.5)

  • (ii)

    for given initial data (ϕ,ψ)(\phi,\psi) and the boundary data h→\vec{h}, the IBVP (1.5) admits at most one mild solution.

More precise statements about these two properties are given below in Theorem 2.5 and Theorem 2.6.

‖(u,v)‖𝒴s≤αr,s​(‖(p,q)‖ℋxs​(ℝ+)+‖(a,b,c)‖ℋts​(ℝ+)),\|(u,v)\|_{{\mathcal{Y}}_{s}}\leq\alpha_{r,s}\left(\|(p,q)\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}+\|(a,b,c)\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\right),

For s∈(−34,3]s\in(-\frac{3}{4},3], (p,q)∈ℋxs​(ℝ+)(p,q)\in\mathcal{H}_{x}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and (a,b,c)∈ℋts​(ℝ+)(a,b,c)\in\mathcal{H}_{t}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}), the IBVP (1.4) admits at most one mild solution (u,v)(u,v) in the sense of Definition 1.1.

‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Xs,σ−1α,β+‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Zs,σ−1α,β\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}}+\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{Z^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq C​‖w1‖Xs,12,σα,β​‖w2‖Xs,12,σ−α,−β.\displaystyle C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}.

The verification of Proposition 2.10 will be presented in Section 5. Then one can take advantage of Proposition 2.8–Proposition 2.10 to justify Theorem 2.3. Based on Theorem 2.3, we will establish the persistence of regularity property in Proposition 6.4 which is the key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 2.5 and Theorem 2.6.

2.2 Application to general KdV-KdV systems

We point out that the approach developed in this paper for the IBVP (1.2) can also be applied to study the IBVPs of general coupled KdV-KdV systems (2.24):

(utvt)+A1​(ux​x​xvx​x​x)+A2​(uxvx)=A3​(u​uxv​vx)+A4​(ux​vu​vx),\begin{pmatrix}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{pmatrix}+A_{1}\begin{pmatrix}u_{xxx}\\ v_{xxx}\end{pmatrix}+A_{2}\begin{pmatrix}u_{x}\\ v_{x}\end{pmatrix}=A_{3}\begin{pmatrix}uu_{x}\\ vv_{x}\end{pmatrix}+A_{4}\begin{pmatrix}u_{x}v\\ uv_{x}\end{pmatrix}, (2.24)

where {Ai}1≤i≤4\{A_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq 4} are 2×22\times 2 real constant matrices and A1A_{1} is diagonalizable: A1=M​(a100a2)​M−1A_{1}=M\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}&0\\ 0&a_{2}\end{pmatrix}M^{-1} with a1​a2≠0a_{1}a_{2}\neq 0. By regarding M−1​(uv)M^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}u\\ v\end{pmatrix} as the new unknown functions (still denoted by uu and vv), the third order terms ux​x​xu_{xxx} and vx​x​xv_{xxx} in system (2.24) can be decoupled such that

{ut+a1​ux​x​x+b11​ux=−b12​vx+c11​u​ux+c12​v​vx+d11​ux​v+d12​u​vx,vt+a2​vx​x​x+b22​vx=−b21​ux+c21​u​ux+c22​v​vx+d21​ux​v+d22​u​vx,\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}+a_{1}u_{xxx}+b_{11}u_{x}&=&-b_{12}v_{x}+c_{11}uu_{x}+c_{12}vv_{x}+d_{11}u_{x}v+d_{12}uv_{x},\\ v_{t}+a_{2}v_{xxx}+b_{22}v_{x}&=&-b_{21}u_{x}+c_{21}uu_{x}+c_{22}vv_{x}+d_{21}u_{x}v+d_{22}uv_{x},\end{array}\right. (2.25)

where the dispersion coefficients a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} are the nonzero eigenvalues of the matrix A1A_{1}. Systems (2.24) include many practical models, such as the well-known Majda-Biello system[MB03], the Hirota-Satsuma system [HS81] and the Gear-Grimshaw system [GG84]. The Cauchy problem for general systems (2.24) posed either on ℝ\mathbb{R} or on the torus 𝕋\mathbb{T} has been well studied in the literature for its well-posedness in the space Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) or Hs​(𝕋)×Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{T}). The interested readers are referred to [YZ22a, YZ22b] and the references therein for an overall review of this study. For the IBVPs of systems (2.24) posed on ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+}, we can justify the well-posedness results similar to that presented in Theorem 1.3 for the IBVP (1.2) using the same approach.

In the following, we list two such results for the IBVPs of the Gear-Grimshaw system (2.26) on ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+}:

{ut+ux​x​x+σ3​vx​x​x=−u​ux+σ1​v​vx+σ2​(u​v)x,ρ1​vt+ρ2​σ3​ux​x​x+vx​x​x+σ4​vx=ρ2​σ2​u​ux−v​vx+ρ2​σ1​(u​v)x,\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+\sigma_{3}v_{xxx}&=&-uu_{x}+\sigma_{1}vv_{x}+\sigma_{2}(uv)_{x},\\ \rho_{1}v_{t}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}u_{xxx}+v_{xxx}+\sigma_{4}v_{x}&=&\rho_{2}\sigma_{2}uu_{x}-vv_{x}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}(uv)_{x},\end{array}\right. (2.26)

where σi∈ℝ⁡(1≤i≤4)\sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R}(1\leq i\leq 4) and ρ1,ρ2>0\rho_{1},\,\rho_{2}>0. This system can be written in the format of (2.24) with

A1=(1σ3ρ2​σ3ρ11ρ1),A2=(000σ4ρ1),A3=(−1σ1ρ2​σ2ρ1−1ρ1),A4=(σ2σ2ρ2​σ1ρ1ρ2​σ1ρ1).A_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\sigma_{3}\\ \frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}}{\rho_{1}}&\frac{1}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix},\quad A_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&\frac{\sigma_{4}}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix},\quad A_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&\sigma_{1}\\ \frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{2}}{\rho_{1}}&-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix},\quad A_{4}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{2}&\sigma_{2}\\ \frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}}{\rho_{1}}&\frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix}.

Note that when ρ2​σ32≠1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}\neq 1, A1A_{1} possesses two nonzero real eigenvalues λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} with λ1≤λ2\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}. Moreover, λ1<0<λ2\lambda_{1}<0<\lambda_{2} if ρ2​σ32>1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}>1; 0<λ1<λ20<\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2} if ρ2​σ32<1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}<1; and λ1=λ2=1\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=1 if σ3=0\sigma_{3}=0 and ρ1=1\rho_{1}=1. Thus, when ρ2​σ32>1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}>1, we need to impose three boundary conditions as that in the case of the IBVP (1.2),

{ut+ux​x​x+σ3​vx​x​x=−u​ux+σ1​v​vx+σ2​(u​v)x,x,t>0,ρ1​vt+ρ2​σ3​ux​x​x+vx​x​x+σ4​vx=ρ2​σ2​u​ux−v​vx+ρ2​σ1​(u​v)x,x,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=ϕ⁡(x),v⁡(x,0)=ψ⁡(x),x>0,u⁡(0,t)=h1​(t),v(0,t)=h2(t),vx(0,t)=h3(t),t>0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcll}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+\sigma_{3}v_{xxx}&=&-uu_{x}+\sigma_{1}vv_{x}+\sigma_{2}(uv)_{x},&x,\ t>0,\\ \rho_{1}v_{t}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}u_{xxx}+v_{xxx}+\sigma_{4}v_{x}&=&\rho_{2}\sigma_{2}uu_{x}-vv_{x}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}(uv)_{x},&x,\ t>0,\\ u(x,0)=\phi(x),&&v(x,0)=\psi(x),&x>0,\\ u(0,t)=h_{1}(t),&&v(0,t)=h_{2}(t),\ v_{x}(0,t)=h_{3}(t),&t>0.\end{array}\right. (2.27)

But in the case of ρ2​σ32<1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}<1, we only need to impose two boundary conditions since λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} have the same sign.

{ut+ux​x​x+σ3​vx​x​x=−u​ux+σ1​v​vx+σ2​(u​v)x,x,t>0,ρ1​vt+ρ2​σ3​ux​x​x+vx​x​x+σ4​vx=ρ2​σ2​u​ux−v​vx+ρ2​σ1​(u​v)x,x,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=ϕ⁡(x),v⁡(x,0)=ψ⁡(x),x>0,u⁡(0,t)=h1​(t),v⁡(0,t)=h2​(t),t>0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcll}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+\sigma_{3}v_{xxx}&=&-uu_{x}+\sigma_{1}vv_{x}+\sigma_{2}(uv)_{x},&x,\ t>0,\\ \rho_{1}v_{t}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}u_{xxx}+v_{xxx}+\sigma_{4}v_{x}&=&\rho_{2}\sigma_{2}uu_{x}-vv_{x}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}(uv)_{x},&x,\ t>0,\\ u(x,0)=\phi(x),&&v(x,0)=\psi(x),&x>0,\\ u(0,t)=h_{1}(t),&&\ v(0,t)=h_{2}(t),&t>0.\end{array}\right. (2.28)

In Theorem 1.6 in [YZ22a], the authors obtained a complete list of well-posedness results for the Cauchy problem of the Gear-Grimshaw system (2.26) posed on ℝ\mathbb{R} for all possibilities of the parameters ρ1\rho_{1}, ρ2\rho_{2} and σi​(1≤i≤4)\sigma_{i}(1\leq i\leq 4). Based on this result and the method we developed to prove Theorem 1.3, we can also establish the following well-posedness results concerning the IBVP of (2.27) or (2.28) on ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+}.

  1. (i)

    s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} if σ3=0\sigma_{3}=0 and ρ1=1\rho_{1}=1;

  2. (ii)

    s≥0s\geq 0 if ρ2​σ32<1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}<1 but (2.29) below is not satisfied;

  3. (iii)

    s≥34s\geq\frac{3}{4} if

    ρ2​σ32≤925,ρ1=12​(α±α2−4)\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}\leq\frac{9}{25},\quad\rho_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha\pm\sqrt{\alpha^{2}-4}\right) (2.29)

    with

    α=17−25​ρ2​σ324.\alpha=\frac{17-25\rho_{2}\sigma^{2}_{3}}{4}.

Finally, we remark that the current paper only studies the 1D Boussinesq systems, however, the 2D Boussinesq systems are also of great importance and has attracted significant attention, see e.g. [BCL05, BLS08, DMS07, MSZ12, SWX17, LPS12]. These earlier works mainly focus on the well-posedness of the 2D Boussinesq systems on the space-time region ℝ2×(0,T)\mathbb{R}^{2}\times(0,T), it might be an interesting future task to study their well-posedness on ℝ+×ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{+}.

2.3 Outline of the remaining paper

  • •

    In Section 3, we will present some results for the Cauchy problem of the KdV equation and the reversed KdV equation posed on the whole line ℝ\mathbb{R} which will play an important role later in dealing with the initial boundary value problems of the coupled KdV systems.

  • •

    In Section 4, we investigate the linear IBVPs (2.16) and (2.17) to carry out the proofs of Proposition 2.8 and Proposition 2.9.

  • •

    In Section 5, various bilinear estimates presented in Proposition 2.10 will be established.

  • •

    Section 6 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.4, the main result of this paper. Equivalently, we will establish Theorems 2.3, 2.5 and 2.6 in Section 6.

|M⁡(μ)|≤C​|(Pβ)′​(μ)|12​⟨μ⟩s+1,∀μ∈ℝ,|M(\mu)|\leq C|(P_{\beta})^{\prime}(\mu)|^{\frac{1}{2}}\langle\mu\rangle^{s+1},\quad\forall\,\mu\in\mathbb{R}, (3.6)

4 Linear problems

In this section, we will study the linear IBVPs (2.16) and (2.17), present the proofs of Proposition 2.8 and Proposition 2.9.

4.1 KdV flow traveling to the right

Consideration is first given to the linear IBVP (2.16) which is copied below for convenience of readers.

{ut+ux​x​x+β​ux=f,u⁡(x,0)=p⁡(x),u⁡(0,t)=a⁡(t),x,t>0.\begin{cases}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+\beta u_{x}=f,\\ u(x,0)=p(x),\\ u(0,t)=a(t),\end{cases}\qquad x,t>0. (4.1)

This system describes a linear dispersive wave traveling to the right, where p∈Hs​(ℝ+)p\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}), a∈Hs+13​(ℝ+)a\in H^{\frac{s+1}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+}), and ff is a function defined on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Next, we will provide an explicit formula (in integral form) for the boundary integral operator Wb​d​r1,β​(a)W^{1,\beta}_{bdr}(a). For any β>0\beta>0, let PβP_{\beta} be as given in (3.5) and define the function Rβ:ℝ→ℂR_{\beta}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C} by

Next, in order to prove (4.16)–(4.18), we decompose 𝒯β​(h)\mathcal{T}_{\beta}(h) as 𝒯β​(h)=𝒯β,1​(h)+𝒯β,2​(h)\mathcal{T}_{\beta}(h)=\mathcal{T}_{\beta,1}(h)+\mathcal{T}_{\beta,2}(h), where

Proof of (4.16).

Firstly, we discuss the estimate for 𝒯β,1​(h)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,1}(h) and we will actually prove a stronger result:

‖η⁡(t)​𝒯β,1​(h)‖X3,11,β≲‖h‖Hs​(ℝ).\|\eta(t)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,1}(h)\|_{X^{1,\beta}_{3,1}}\lesssim\|h\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R})}. (4.23)

Next we discuss the estimate for 𝒯β,2​(h)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,2}(h) which is further decomposed into two parts: 𝒯β,2​(h)=𝒯β,3​(h)+𝒯β,4​(h)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,2}(h)=\mathcal{T}_{\beta,3}(h)+\mathcal{T}_{\beta,4}(h), where

[𝒯β,3​(h)]​(x,t)\displaystyle[\mathcal{T}_{\beta,3}(h)](x,t) :=∫43​β4ei​Pβ​(μ)​te−iμx/2k(Rβ(μ)x)h^(μ)dμ,\displaystyle:=\int\limits_{\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}\beta}}^{4}e^{iP_{\beta}(\mu)t}e^{-i\mu x/2}k\big(R_{\beta}(\mu)x\big)\,\widehat{h}(\mu)\,d\mu, (4.24)
[𝒯β,4​(h)]​(x,t)\displaystyle[\mathcal{T}_{\beta,4}(h)](x,t) :=∫4∞ei​Pβ​(μ)​te−iμx/2k(Rβ(μ)x)h^(μ)dμ.\displaystyle:=\int\limits_{4}^{\infty}e^{iP_{\beta}(\mu)t}e^{-i\mu x/2}k\big(R_{\beta}(\mu)x\big)\,\widehat{h}(\mu)\,d\mu. (4.25)

The reason of introducing such a decomposition is to make sure that Rβ​(μ)R_{\beta}(\mu) has a positive lower bound in 𝒯β,4​(h)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,4}(h). For example, with the choice of 4, we have Rβ​(μ)>3R_{\beta}(\mu)>3 for any μ≥4\mu\geq 4 since 0<β≤10<\beta\leq 1. The choice of the cut-off number 4 is flexible, as long as it is away from 43​β\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}\beta}. For the estimate on 𝒯β,3\mathcal{T}_{\beta,3}, we will also prove a stronger result:

‖η⁡(t)​𝒯β,3​(h)‖X3,11,β≲‖h‖Hs​(ℝ).\|\eta(t)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,3}(h)\|_{X^{1,\beta}_{3,1}}\lesssim\|h\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R})}. (4.26)

So the focus is turned to the estimate on ‖η⁡(t)​𝒯β,4​(h)‖Xs,121,β\|\eta(t)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,4}(h)\|_{X^{1,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2}}}. By direct computation,

Since kk is a Schwarz function, so is k^\widehat{k}, hence,

|k^​(ξ+μ/2Rβ​(μ))|≲Rβ6​(μ)Rβ6​(μ)+|ξ+μ/2|6∼μ6μ6+|2​ξ+μ|6.\left|\widehat{k}\left(\frac{\xi+\mu/2}{R_{\beta}(\mu)}\right)\right|\lesssim\frac{R_{\beta}^{6}(\mu)}{R_{\beta}^{6}(\mu)+|\xi+\mu/2|^{6}}\sim\frac{\mu^{6}}{\mu^{6}+|2\xi+\mu|^{6}}.

For any μ≥4\mu\geq 4, ⟨τ−ϕ1,β​(ξ)⟩≤⟨τ−Pβ​(μ)⟩​⟨Pβ​(μ)−ϕ1,β​(ξ)⟩≲⟨τ−Pβ​(μ)⟩​(μ+|ξ|)3\langle\tau-\phi^{1,\beta}(\xi)\rangle\leq\langle\tau-P_{\beta}(\mu)\rangle\langle P_{\beta}(\mu)-\phi^{1,\beta}(\xi)\rangle\lesssim\langle\tau-P_{\beta}(\mu)\rangle(\mu+|\xi|)^{3}, so it follows from (4.27) that

This leads to

|ℱ⁡[η⁡(t)​𝒯β,4​(h)]​(ξ,τ)|≲∫4∞|η^​(τ−Pβ​(μ))|​μ−1​|h^​(μ)|​𝑑μ.\big|\mathcal{F}[\eta(t)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,4}(h)](\xi,\tau)\big|\lesssim\int_{4}^{\infty}\left|\widehat{\eta}\big(\tau-P_{\beta}(\mu)\big)\right|\,\mu^{-1}|\widehat{h}(\mu)|\,d\mu.

‖η⁡(t)​𝒯β​(h)‖Λs,σ1,β=‖𝟙{e|ξ|≤3+|τ|}⟨ξ⟩s⟨τ−ϕα,β(ξ)⟩σℱ[η(t)𝒯β,4(h)](ξ,τ)‖Lξ,τ2≲‖∫4∞⟨τ⟩σ+ϵ1​|η^​(τ−Pβ​(μ))|​μ−1​|h^​(μ)|​dμ‖Lτ2.\begin{split}\big\|\eta(t)\mathcal{T}_{\beta}(h)\big\|_{\Lambda^{1,\beta}_{s,\sigma}}&=\left\|\mathbbm{1}_{\{e^{|\xi|}\leq 3+|\tau|\}}\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\phi^{\alpha,\beta}(\xi)\rangle^{\sigma}\mathcal{F}[\eta(t)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,4}(h)](\xi,\tau)\right\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}}\\ &\lesssim\left\|\int_{4}^{\infty}\langle\tau\rangle^{\sigma+\epsilon_{1}}\left|\widehat{\eta}\big(\tau-P_{\beta}(\mu)\big)\right|\mu^{-1}|\widehat{h}(\mu)|\,d\mu\right\|_{L^{2}_{\tau}}.\end{split} (4.33)

ϵ1=2​s+112\epsilon_{1}=\frac{2s+1}{12} (4.34)

fulfills this requirement thanks to the restriction σ≤2​s+712\sigma\leq\frac{2s+7}{12}. ∎

Proof of (4.18).

Again, based on the proof of (4.16), it will not take significantly more effort to verify (4.18), but we will still carry out its proof with the purose of revealing the necessity of the assumption s>−12s>-\frac{1}{2} in Lemma 4.3. It thus remains to estimate ‖η⁡(t)​𝒯β,4​(h)‖Lt∞​Hxs\|\eta(t)\mathcal{T}_{\beta,4}(h)\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}H^{s}_{x}}. ‖[𝒯β,4​(h)]​(x,0)‖Hxs=‖⟨ξ⟩s​∫4∞k^​(ξ+μ/2Rβ​(μ))​h^​(μ)Rβ​(μ)​𝑑μ‖Lξ2.\left\|\big[\mathcal{T}_{\beta,4}(h)\big](x,0)\right\|_{H^{s}_{x}}=\left\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\int_{4}^{\infty}\widehat{k}\left(\frac{\xi+\mu/2}{R_{\beta}(\mu)}\right)\frac{\widehat{h}(\mu)}{R_{\beta}(\mu)}\,d\mu\right\|_{L^{2}_{\xi}}.

(4.35)

Exchanging the order of integration and shifting ξ\xi, we obtain

∫ℝ∫4∞g⁡(ξ)​⟨ξ⟩s​k^​(ξ+μ/2Rβ​(μ))​h^​(μ)Rβ​(μ)​dμ​dξ=∫4∞∫ℝg⁡(ξ−μ2)​⟨ξ−μ2⟩s​k^​(ξRβ​(μ))​h^​(μ)Rβ​(μ)​dξ​dμ.\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{4}^{\infty}g(\xi)\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\widehat{k}\Big(\frac{\xi+\mu/2}{R_{\beta}(\mu)}\Big)\frac{\widehat{h}(\mu)}{R_{\beta}(\mu)}d\mu d\xi=\int_{4}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}}g\Big(\xi-\frac{\mu}{2}\Big)\left\langle\xi-\frac{\mu}{2}\right\rangle^{s}\widehat{k}\Big(\frac{\xi}{R_{\beta}(\mu)}\Big)\frac{\widehat{h}(\mu)}{R_{\beta}(\mu)}d\xi d\mu.\end{split} (4.36)

The rest proof can be carried out by a parallel argument as that for Proposition 2.8 except we apply Lemmas 4.8, 4.10 and 4.11 instead of Lemmas 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4 respectively.

5 Bilinear Estimates

This section is intended to prove Proposition 2.10. Since b≤12b\leq\frac{1}{2} is required to deal with the boundary integral operators, it brings two issues. First, the bilinear estimate may not be justified in the space Xs,bα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b} via the classical methods as in [Bou93b, KPV93, KPV96]. Secondly, Xs,bα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b} is not a subspace of Ct​(ℝ,Hxs)C_{t}\big(\mathbb{R};H^{s}_{x}\big), so living in Xs,bα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b} may not guarantee the continuity of the solution flow. In order to overcome these two barriers, we will take advantage of the modified Fourier restriction spaces as defined in (2.6) and (2.7). On the other hand, as it is well-known that the resonance function plays an essential role in the bilinear estimates, so we first specify its definition, see e.g. [Tao01].

Definition 5.1 ([Tao01]).

Let ((α1,β1),(α2,β2),(α3,β3))\big((\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}),(\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}),(\alpha_{3},\beta_{3})\big) be a triple in ((ℝ\{0})×ℝ)3((\mathbb{R}\backslash\{0\})\times\mathbb{R})^{3}. Define the resonance function HH associated to this triple by

H⁡(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=∑i=13ϕαi,βi​(ξi),∀(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)∈ℝ3​with​∑i=13ξi=0,H(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\phi^{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}}(\xi_{i}),\quad\forall\,(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\,\,\text{with}\,\,\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0, (5.1)

where ϕ\phi is defined as in (2.3).

Since Proposition 2.10 contains many inequalities, we split its proof into three parts for the sake of clarity, see the following Proposition 5.2–Proposition 5.4.

Proposition 5.2.

Let −34<s≤3-\frac{3}{4}<s\leq 3, α≠0\alpha\neq 0 and |β|≤1|\beta|\leq 1. Then there exists σ0=σ0​(s,α)>12\sigma_{0}=\sigma_{0}(s,\alpha)>\frac{1}{2} such that for any σ∈(12,σ0]\sigma\in(\frac{1}{2},\sigma_{0}], the following bilinear estimates

‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Xs,σ−1α,β\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq C​‖w1‖Xs,12,σα,β​‖w2‖Xs,12,σα,β\displaystyle C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}} (5.2)
‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Zs,σ−1α,β\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{Z^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq C​‖w1‖Xs,12,σα,β​‖w2‖Xs,12,σα,β\displaystyle C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}} (5.3)

hold for any w1,w2∈Xs,12,σα,βw_{1},w_{2}\in X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma} with some constant C=C⁡(s,α,σ)C=C(s,\alpha,\sigma).

‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Xs,σ−1−α,−β\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq C​‖w1‖Xs,12,σα,β​‖w2‖Xs,12,σα,β\displaystyle C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}} (5.4)
‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Zs,σ−1−α,−β\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{Z^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq C​‖w1‖Xs,12,σα,β​‖w2‖Xs,12,σα,β\displaystyle C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}} (5.5)

hold for any w1,w2∈Xs,12,σα,βw_{1},w_{2}\in X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma} with some constant C=C⁡(s,α,σ)C=C(s,\alpha,\sigma).

Proposition 5.4.

Let −34<s≤3-\frac{3}{4}<s\leq 3, α≠0\alpha\neq 0 and |β|≤1|\beta|\leq 1. Then there exists σ0=σ0​(s,α)>12\sigma_{0}=\sigma_{0}(s,\alpha)>\frac{1}{2} such that for any σ∈(12,σ0]\sigma\in(\frac{1}{2},\sigma_{0}], the following bilinear estimates

‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Xs,σ−1α,β\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq C​‖w1‖Xs,12,σα,β​‖w2‖Xs,12,σ−α,−β\displaystyle C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}} (5.6)

hold for any w1∈Xs,12,σα,βw_{1}\in X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma} and w2∈Xs,12,σ−α,−βw_{2}\in X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma} with some constant C=C⁡(s,α,σ)C=C(s,\alpha,\sigma).

The proofs for these three propositions are similar while Proposition 5.4 is slightly more challenging since w1w_{1} and w2w_{2} live in different spaces. As a result, we will only prove Proposition 5.4. Before the proof, we first recall some elementary technical results.

Lemma 5.5.

Let ρ1≥ρ2>12\rho_{1}\geq\rho_{2}>\frac{1}{2} and ρ3∈ℝ\rho_{3}\in\mathbb{R} satisfy

{ρ3=ρ2ifρ1>1,ρ3<ρ2ifρ1=1,ρ3=ρ1+ρ2−1if12<ρ1<1,\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcc}\rho_{3}=\rho_{2}&\text{if}&\rho_{1}>1,\\ \rho_{3}<\rho_{2}&\text{if}&\rho_{1}=1,\\ \rho_{3}=\rho_{1}+\rho_{2}-1&\text{if}&\frac{1}{2}<\rho_{1}<1,\end{array}\right.

then there exists C=C⁡(ρ1,ρ2,ρ3)C=C(\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\rho_{3}) such that for any a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R},

∫−∞∞d​x⟨x−a⟩ρ1​⟨−x−b⟩ρ2≤C⟨a+b⟩ρ3.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle x-a\rangle^{\rho_{1}}\langle-x-b\rangle^{\rho_{2}}}\leq\frac{C}{\langle a+b\rangle^{\rho_{3}}}. (5.8)

The proof for this lemma is standard (see e.g. [ET16, KPV96]) and therefore omitted, we just want to remark that ⟨a+b⟩=⟨(x−a)+(−x−b)⟩\langle a+b\rangle=\langle(x-a)+(-x-b)\rangle.

Lemma 5.6.

If ρ>12\rho>\frac{1}{2}, then there exists C=C⁡(ρ)C=C(\rho) such that for any σi∈ℝ\sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R} (0≤i≤2)(0\leq i\leq 2) with σ2≠0\sigma_{2}\neq 0,

∫−∞∞d​x⟨σ2​x2+σ1​x+σ0⟩ρ≤C|σ2|1/2.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle\sigma_{2}x^{2}+\sigma_{1}x+\sigma_{0}\rangle^{\rho}}\leq\frac{C}{|\sigma_{2}|^{1/2}}. (5.9)

Similarly, if ρ>13\rho>\frac{1}{3}, then there exists C=C⁡(ρ)C=C(\rho) such that for any σi∈ℝ\sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R} (0≤i≤3)(0\leq i\leq 3) with σ3≠0\sigma_{3}\neq 0,

∫−∞∞d​x⟨σ3​x3+σ2​x2+σ1​x+σ0⟩ρ≤C|σ3|1/3.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle\sigma_{3}x^{3}+\sigma_{2}x^{2}+\sigma_{1}x+\sigma_{0}\rangle^{\rho}}\leq\frac{C}{|\sigma_{3}|^{1/3}}. (5.10)
Proof.

We refer the reader to the proof of Lemma 2.5 in [BOP97] where (5.10) was proved. The similar argument can also be applied to obtain (5.9). ∎

σ≤min⁡{ρ+13,712−ρ9}.\sigma\leq\min\Big\{\frac{\rho+1}{3},\,\frac{7}{12}-\frac{\rho}{9}\Big\}. (5.25)

The remaining proof will be divided into three cases depending on the size of the resonance function HH. The first case is when ∑i=13|ξi|\sum_{i=1}^{3}|\xi_{i}| is small which does not ganrantee the estimate (5.20). The second case is when ∑i=13|ξi|\sum_{i=1}^{3}|\xi_{i}| is large enough but |ξ2||\xi_{2}| is small, so although the estimate (5.20) holds, the lower bound in (5.20) may be small. It is this step that forces to use the modified Fourier restriction space. The last case is when ∑i=13|ξi|\sum_{i=1}^{3}|\xi_{i}| is large enough and |ξ2||\xi_{2}| is not too small, so estimate (5.20) holds with a large lower bound. In the following, we will show more details.

σ≤23−2​ρ9.\sigma\leq\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2\rho}{9}. (5.43)

Taking advantage of Proposition 2.8 and Proposition 2.9, we conclude that u∈Ys,12,σ1,β​(Ω1)∩Cxj​(ℝ0+,Hts+1−j3​(ℝ+))u\in Y^{1,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}(\Omega_{1})\cap C_{x}^{j}\big(\mathbb{R}^{+}_{0};H_{t}^{\frac{s+1-j}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\big) and v∈Ys,12,σ−1,−β​(Ω1)∩Cxj​(ℝ0+,Hts+1−j3​(ℝ+))v\in Y^{-1,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}(\Omega_{1})\cap C_{x}^{j}\big(\mathbb{R}^{+}_{0};H_{t}^{\frac{s+1-j}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\big) for j=0,1j=0,1. Now we turn to consider the unconditional well-posedness for the IBVP (1.5) and prove Theorem 2.5 and Theorem 2.6 . Note first that by scaling argument, Theorem 2.3 can be restated as the following result.

Corollary 6.1 (Conditional Well-posedness).

Let −34<s≤3-\frac{3}{4}<s\leq 3, r>0r>0 and 0≤β≤10\leq\beta\leq 1 be given. There exist σ=σ⁡(s)>12\sigma=\sigma(s)>\frac{1}{2} and T=T⁡(s,r)>0T=T(s,r)>0 such that for any naturally compatible (ϕ,ψ)∈ℋxs​(ℝ+)(\phi,\psi)\in{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and h→=(h1,h2,h3)∈ℋts​(ℝ+)\vec{h}=(h_{1},h_{2},h_{3})\in{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) related to the IBVP (1.5) with

∥ϕ,ψ)∥ℋxs​(ℝ+)+∥h→∥ℋts​(ℝ+)≤r,\|\phi,\psi)\|_{{\cal H}^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}+\|\vec{h}\|_{{\cal H}^{s}_{t}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\leq r,

the system of the integral equations (SIE) (2.11) admits a unique solution

(u,v)∈𝒴σ​(ΩT):=Ys,12,σ1,β​(ΩT)×Ys,12,σ−1,−β​(ΩT).(u,v)\in\mathcal{Y}_{\sigma}(\Omega_{T}):=Y^{1,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}(\Omega_{T})\times Y^{-1,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}(\Omega_{T}).

Moreover, the solution map is real analytic in the corresponding spaces.

By standard extension arguments, the solutions given in Corollary 6.1 possess a blow-up alternative property as described below.

Lemma 6.2 (Blow-up alternative).

Let −34<s≤3-\frac{3}{4}<s\leq 3 be given. For any given

(p,q)∈ℋxs​(ℝ+),(a,b,c)∈ℋts​(ℝ+),(p,q)\in\mathcal{H}_{x}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}),\quad(a,b,c)\in\mathcal{H}_{t}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}),

 either Tm​a​xs=+∞ or ​limt→Tmaxs(‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖Hs​(ℝ+)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖Hs​(ℝ+))=+∞.\mbox{ either \hskip 10.22217pt$T^{s}_{max}=+\infty$ \hskip 10.22217ptor \hskip 10.22217pt}\lim_{t\to T^{s}_{\max}}\left(\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\right)=+\infty.

We then intend to prove Theorem 2.5, that is to show the solution (u,v)(u,v) given in Corollary 6.1 is a mild solution of the IBVP (1.4). According to Definition 1.1, mild solutions can be regarded as limits of classical solutions. So we first recall a well-known result about classical solutions.

Lemma 6.3 (Existence and uniqueness of classical solutions).

Let r>0r>0 be given. There exists a T>0T>0 such that for compatible set (p,q)∈ℋx3​(ℝ+)(p,q)\in\mathcal{H}_{x}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and (a,b,c)∈ℋt3​(ℝ+)(a,b,c)\in\mathcal{H}_{t}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) with

‖((p,q))‖ℋx3​(ℝ+)+‖(a,b,c)‖ℋt3​(ℝ+)≤r,\|((p,q))\|_{\mathcal{H}_{x}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}+\|(a,b,c)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{t}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{+})}\leq r,

the IBVP (1.4) admits a unique strong solution (u,v)(u,v) such that both uu and vv belong to C2​(0,T,L2​(ℝ+))∩C⁡(0,T,H3​(ℝ+))C^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{+}))\cap C(0,T;H^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{+})).

Proof.

The existence of the classical solution (u,v)(u,v) follows directly from Corollary 6.1 with s=3s=3, and the uniqueness of the solution can be proved using the standard energy estimate method. ∎

Based on the notations in Lemma 6.2, it can be readily checked that Tm​a​xs1≥Tm​a​xs2T_{max}^{s_{1}}\geq T_{max}^{s_{2}} for s1<s2s_{1}<s_{2}. We then propose that Tm​a​xs1=Tm​a​xs2T_{max}^{s_{1}}=T_{max}^{s_{2}}.

The combination of Corollary 6.1 through Proposition 6.4 enables one to justify Theorem 2.5.

Proof of Theorem 2.5.

According to Corollary 6.1, for given (p,q)∈ℋxs​(ℝ+)(p,q)\in\mathcal{H}_{x}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and (a,b,c)∈ℋts​(ℝ+)(a,b,c)\in\mathcal{H}_{t}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}), one can obtain a solution (u,v)∈Ys,12,σ1,1​(ΩT)×Ys,12,σ−1,−1​(ΩT)(u,v)\in Y^{1,1}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}(\Omega_{T})\times Y^{-1,-1}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}(\Omega_{T}). (un(1),vn(1))=(u~n(1),v~n(1)),(un(2),vn(2))=(u~n(2),v~n(2)),in [C(0,T∗;H3(ℝ+))]2,(u^{(1)}_{n},v^{(1)}_{n})=(\widetilde{u}_{n}^{(1)},\widetilde{v}_{n}^{(1)}),\quad(u^{(2)}_{n},v^{(2)}_{n})=(\widetilde{u}_{n}^{(2)},\widetilde{v}_{n}^{(2)}),\quad\mbox{in }[C(0,T^{*};H^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{+}))]^{2},

due to the uniqueness of the classic solution of the IBVP (1.4). Moreover, according to the continuity of the solution map in Corollary 6.1, one has

limn→∞(u~n(1),v~n(1))=(u~,v~),limn→∞(u~n(2),v~n(2))=(u~,v~),in [C(0,T∗;Hs(ℝ+))]2.\lim_{n\to\infty}(\widetilde{u}_{n}^{(1)},\widetilde{v}_{n}^{(1)})=(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}),\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}(\widetilde{u}_{n}^{(2)},\widetilde{v}_{n}^{(2)})=(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}),\quad\mbox{in }[C(0,T^{*};H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}))]^{2}.

Therefore, we deduce that (u(1),v(1))=(u~,v~)=(u(2),v(2))(u^{(1)},v^{(1)})=(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})=(u^{(2)},v^{(2)}) in [C⁡(0,T∗,Hs​(ℝ+))]2[C(0,T^{*};H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{+}))]^{2}. Finally, we can use continuity property of the solutions (u(1),v(1))(u^{(1)},v^{(1)}), (u(2),v(2))(u^{(2)},v^{(2)}) and (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) to show T1=T2=T3T_{1}=T_{2}=T_{3}. ∎

Appendix A Proofs of Lemma 6.5–Lemma 6.7

The proofs for Lemma 6.5, Lemma 6.6 and Lemma 6.7 are similar, so we will only prove Lemma 6.7. In order to make the argument more clearly, we first present several auxiliary results. We start with the following Lemma A.1 which is a refinement of Proposition 5.4 on the temporal regularity of the term (u​v)x(uv)_{x}.

Lemma A.1.

Let −34<s≤3-\frac{3}{4}<s\leq 3, α≠0\alpha\neq 0 and |β|≤1|\beta|\leq 1. Then there exists ϵ0=ϵ0​(s,α)>0\epsilon_{0}=\epsilon_{0}(s,\alpha)>0 such that for any σ∈(12,12+ϵ0]\sigma\in(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_{0}],

‖(u​v)x‖Xs,σ−1+ϵ0α,β≤C​‖u‖Xs,12,σα,β​‖v‖Xs,12,σ−α,−β,\|(uv)_{x}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1+\epsilon_{0}}}\leq C\|u\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|v\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}, (A.1)

where C=C⁡(s,α,σ)C=C(s,\alpha,\sigma).

Proof.

By duality, it suffices to prove

∬ℝ2ξ​u​v^​w^​𝑑ξ​𝑑τ≤C​‖u‖Xs,12,σα,β​‖v‖Xs,12,σ−α,−β​‖w‖X−s,1−σ−ϵ0α,β,\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\xi\,\widehat{uv}\widehat{w}\,d\xi\,d\tau\leq C\|u\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|v\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{-s,1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}},

for any u∈Xs,12,σα,βu\in X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}, v∈Xs,12,σ−α,−βv\in X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma} and w∈X−s,1−σ−ϵ0α,βw\in X^{\alpha,\beta}_{-s,1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}. Similar to the proof of Proposition 5.4, we denote

L1=τ1−ϕα,β​(ξ1),L2=τ2−ϕ−α,−β​(ξ2),L3=τ3−ϕα,β​(ξ3).L_{1}=\tau_{1}-\phi^{\alpha,\beta}(\xi_{1}),\quad L_{2}=\tau_{2}-\phi^{-\alpha,-\beta}(\xi_{2}),\quad L_{3}=\tau_{3}-\phi^{\alpha,\beta}(\xi_{3}).

and

M1=⟨L1⟩12+𝟙{e|ξ1|≤3+|τ1|}⟨L1⟩σ,M2=⟨L2⟩12+𝟙{e|ξ2|≤3+|τ2|}⟨L2⟩σ.M_{1}=\langle L_{1}\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}}+\mathbbm{1}_{\{e^{|\xi_{1}|}\leq 3+|\tau_{1}|\}}\langle L_{1}\rangle^{\sigma},\quad M_{2}=\langle L_{2}\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}}+\mathbbm{1}_{\{e^{|\xi_{2}|}\leq 3+|\tau_{2}|\}}\langle L_{2}\rangle^{\sigma}.

In addition, we define

f1(ξ1,τ1)=⟨ξ1⟩sM1u^(ξ1,τ1),f2(ξ2,τ2)=⟨ξ2⟩sM2v^(ξ2,τ2),f3​(ξ3,τ3)=⟨ξ3⟩−s​⟨L3⟩1−σ−ϵ0​w^​(ξ3,τ3).\begin{array}[]{c}f_{1}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})=\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}M_{1}\widehat{u}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1}),\quad f_{2}(\xi_{2},\tau_{2})=\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}M_{2}\widehat{v}(\xi_{2},\tau_{2}),\\ f_{3}(\xi_{3},\tau_{3})=\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{-s}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}\widehat{w}(\xi_{3},\tau_{3}).\end{array}

Then it reduces to justify

∫A|ξ3|​⟨ξ1⟩ρ​⟨ξ2⟩ρ​∏i=13|fi​(ξi,τi)|⟨ξ3⟩ρ​M1​M2​⟨L3⟩1−σ−ϵ0≤C​∏i=13‖fi‖Lξ​τ2,\int\limits_{A}\frac{|\xi_{3}|\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{\rho}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{\rho}\prod\limits_{i=1}^{3}|f_{i}(\xi_{i},\tau_{i})|}{\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{\rho}M_{1}M_{2}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}}\leq C\,\prod_{i=1}^{3}\|f_{i}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}, (A.2)

where ρ=−s\rho=-s and the set AA is as defined in (5.11). In the remaining proof, instead of introducing σ0\sigma_{0} as in (5.24), we define ϵ0=116−112​ρ\epsilon_{0}=\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{12}\,\rho. Then for any σ∈(12,12+ϵ0]\sigma\in(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_{0}], (A.2) can be proved in an analogous way as the proof of (5.6) in Proposition 5.4.

∎

Next, we will take advantage of Proposition A.1 to deduce a slightly stronger estimate since the spatial regularity requirement on the right-hand side of (A.3) is weaker than that of (A.1).

Lemma A.2.

Let −34<s1≤s2≤3-\frac{3}{4}<s_{1}\leq s_{2}\leq 3, α≠0\alpha\neq 0, |β|≤1|\beta|\leq 1. Then there exists ϵ0=ϵ0​(s1,s2,α)>0\epsilon_{0}=\epsilon_{0}(s_{1},s_{2},\alpha)>0 such that for any σ∈(12,12+ϵ0]\sigma\in(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_{0}],

‖(u​v)x‖Xs2,σ−1+ϵ0α,β≤C⁡(‖u‖Xs1,12,σα,β​‖v‖Xs2,12,σ−α,−β+‖u‖Xs2,12,σα,β​‖v‖Xs1,12,σ−α,−β),\|(uv)_{x}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\sigma-1+\epsilon_{0}}}\leq C\Big(\|u\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{1},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|v\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}+\|u\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|v\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{1},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\Big), (A.3)

where C=C⁡(s1,s2,α,σ)C=C(s_{1},s_{2},\alpha,\sigma).

Proof.

By duality, it suffices to prove

∬ℝ2ξ​u​v^​w^​𝑑ξ​𝑑τ≤C⁡(‖u‖Xs1,12,σα,β​‖v‖Xs2,12,σ−α,−β+‖u‖Xs2,12,σα,β​‖v‖Xs1,12,σ−α,−β)​‖w‖X−s2,1−σ−ϵ0α,β,\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\xi\,\widehat{uv}\widehat{w}\,d\xi\,d\tau\leq C\Big(\|u\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{1},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|v\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}+\|u\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|v\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{1},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\Big)\|w\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{-s_{2},1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}},

for any u∈Xs2,12,σα,βu\in X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}, v∈Xs2,12,σ−α,−βv\in X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma} and w∈X−s2,1−σ−ϵ0α,βw\in X^{\alpha,\beta}_{-s_{2},1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}. Denote L1,L2,L3,M1,M2L_{1},L_{2},L_{3},M_{1},M_{2} in the same way as the above proof for Lemma A.1, and define

f1(ξ1,τ1)=⟨ξ1⟩s1M1u^(ξ1,τ1),f2(ξ2,τ2)=⟨ξ2⟩s1M2v^(ξ2,τ2),f3(ξ3,τ3)=⟨ξ3⟩−s2⟨L3⟩1−σ−ϵ0w^(ξ3,τ3).\begin{array}[]{c}f_{1}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})=\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s_{1}}M_{1}\widehat{u}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1}),\ \,f_{2}(\xi_{2},\tau_{2})=\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s_{1}}M_{2}\widehat{v}(\xi_{2},\tau_{2}),\ \,f_{3}(\xi_{3},\tau_{3})=\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{-s_{2}}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}\widehat{w}(\xi_{3},\tau_{3}).\end{array}

Denote ρ=−s1\rho=-s_{1} and r=s2−s1≥0r=s_{2}-s_{1}\geq 0. Then similar to (A.2), it reduces to show

∫A⟨ξ3⟩r​|ξ3​|⟨ξ1⟩ρ​⟨ξ2⟩ρ|​f1​(ξ1,τ1)​f2​(ξ2,τ2)​f3​(ξ3,τ3)|⟨ξ3⟩ρ​M1​M2​⟨L3⟩1−σ−ϵ0≤C⁡(‖f1‖Lξ​τ2​‖⟨ξ⟩r​f2‖Lξ​τ2+‖⟨ξ⟩r​f1‖Lξ​τ2​‖f2‖Lξ​τ2)​‖f3‖Lξ​τ2.\begin{split}&\quad\,\int\limits_{A}\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{r}\frac{|\xi_{3}|\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{\rho}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{\rho}|f_{1}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})f_{2}(\xi_{2},\tau_{2})f_{3}(\xi_{3},\tau_{3})|}{\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{\rho}M_{1}M_{2}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}}\\ &\leq C\,\Big(\|f_{1}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}\|\langle\xi\rangle^{r}f_{2}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}+\|\langle\xi\rangle^{r}f_{1}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}\|f_{2}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}\Big)\|f_{3}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}.\end{split} (A.4)

Since r≥0r\geq 0 and ∑i=13ξi=0\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0, then ⟨ξ3⟩r=⟨ξ1+ξ2⟩r≤2r​(⟨ξ1⟩r+⟨ξ2⟩r)\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{r}=\langle\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}\rangle^{r}\leq 2^{r}\big(\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{r}+\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{r}\big). I​I=∫A|ξ3​|⟨ξ1⟩ρ​⟨ξ2⟩ρ|​f1​(ξ1,τ1)|​|⟨ξ2⟩r​f2​(ξ2,τ2)​f3​(ξ3,τ3)|⟨ξ3⟩ρ​M1​M2​⟨L3⟩1−σ−ϵ0.\displaystyle II=\int\limits_{A}\frac{|\xi_{3}|\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{\rho}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{\rho}|f_{1}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})|\,|\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{r}f_{2}(\xi_{2},\tau_{2})f_{3}(\xi_{3},\tau_{3})|}{\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{\rho}M_{1}M_{2}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-\sigma-\epsilon_{0}}}.

According to Lemma A.1,

I≤C​‖⟨ξ⟩r​f1‖Lξ​τ2​‖f2‖Lξ​τ2​‖f3‖Lξ​τ2,I​I≤C​‖f1‖Lξ​τ2​‖⟨ξ⟩r​f2‖Lξ​τ2​‖f3‖Lξ​τ2.I\leq C\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^{r}f_{1}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}\|f_{2}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}\|f_{3}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}},\quad II\leq C\,\|f_{1}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}\|\langle\xi\rangle^{r}f_{2}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}\|f_{3}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}}.

Thus, (A.4) is verified. ∎

Recalling the cut-off function η∈C0∞​(ℝ)\eta\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R}) which satisfies η⁡(t)=1\eta(t)=1 on (−1,1)(-1,1) and supp​η⊂(−2,2)\text{supp}\,\eta\subset(-2,2), the following is a classical estimate on the Fourier restriction norms when the time is localized.

Lemma A.3.

For any s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, −12<b1≤b2<12-\frac{1}{2}<b_{1}\leq b_{2}<\frac{1}{2}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0, |β|≤1|\beta|\leq 1 and 0<T≤10<T\leq 1, there exists a constant C=C⁡(s,b1,b2)C=C(s,b_{1},b_{2}) such that

‖η⁡(tT)​w‖Xs,b1α,β≤C​Tb2−b1​‖w‖Xs,b2α,β,∀w∈Xs,b2α,β.\Big\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)w\Big\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b_{1}}}\leq C\,T^{b_{2}-b_{1}}\|w\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b_{2}}},\quad\forall\,w\in X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b_{2}}. (A.5)

The proof of this estimate is well-known, see e.g. Lemma 2.11 in [Tao06]. Combining Lemma A.2 and Lemma A.3 yields the outcome below.

Lemma A.4.

Let −34<s1≤s2≤3-\frac{3}{4}<s_{1}\leq s_{2}\leq 3, α≠0\alpha\neq 0, |β|≤1|\beta|\leq 1 and 0<T≤10<T\leq 1. Then there exists ϵ0=ϵ0​(s1,s2,α)>0\epsilon_{0}=\epsilon_{0}(s_{1},s_{2},\alpha)>0 such that for any σ∈(12,12+ϵ0]\sigma\in(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_{0}],

‖η⁡(tT)​(u​v)x‖Xs2,σ−1α,β≤C​Tϵ0​(‖u‖Xs1,12,σα,β​‖v‖Xs2,12,σ−α,−β+‖u‖Xs2,12,σα,β​‖v‖Xs1,12,σ−α,−β),\Big\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)(uv)_{x}\Big\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\sigma-1}}\leq CT^{\epsilon_{0}}\Big(\|u\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{1},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|v\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}+\|u\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|v\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{1},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\Big), (A.6)

where C=C⁡(s1,s2,α,σ)C=C(s_{1},s_{2},\alpha,\sigma).

Proof.

Firstly, we choose ϵ0\epsilon_{0} as that in Lemma A.2. Then for any σ∈(12,12+ϵ0]\sigma\in(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_{0}], we choose w=(u​v)xw=(uv)_{x}, s=s2s=s_{2}, b1=σ−1b_{1}=\sigma-1 and b2=σ−1+ϵ0b_{2}=\sigma-1+\epsilon_{0} in (A.5) to obtain

‖η⁡(tT)​(u​v)x‖Xs2,σ−1α,β≤C​Tϵ0​‖(u​v)x‖Xs2,σ−1α,β.\Big\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)(uv)_{x}\Big\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\sigma-1}}\leq CT^{\epsilon_{0}}\|(uv)_{x}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\sigma-1}}.

Then we can apply Lemma A.2 to verify (A.6). ∎

Similar to Lemma A.3, the estimate for modified Fourier restriction norms of the localized (in time) Duhamel term associated with the semigroup operator WRα,βW^{\alpha,\beta}_{R} can also be established.

Lemma A.5.

Let s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0, |β|≤1|\beta|\leq 1, 12<σ<1\frac{1}{2}<\sigma<1 and 0<T≤10<T\leq 1. Then there exists a constant C=C⁡(s,α,σ)C=C(s,\alpha,\sigma) such that

‖η⁡(tT)​∫0tWRα,β​(t−τ)​F​𝑑τ‖Xs,12,σα,β≤C​‖η⁡(t2​T)​F‖Xs,σ−1α,β.\left\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)\int^{t}_{0}W_{R}^{\alpha,\beta}(t-\tau)F\,d\tau\right\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\leq C\Big\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{2T}\Big)F\Big\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}}. (A.7)
Proof.

Define g⁡(x,t)=η⁡(t2​T)​F​(x,t)g(x,t)=\eta\big(\frac{t}{2T}\big)F(x,t). Then it is easily seen that

LHS of (A.7) =‖η⁡(tT)​∫0tWRα,β​(t−τ)​g​𝑑τ‖Xs,12,σα,β.\displaystyle=\left\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)\int^{t}_{0}W_{R}^{\alpha,\beta}(t-\tau)g\,d\tau\right\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}.

Then similar to Lemma 3.4 (also see Lemma 2.1 in [GTV97]), we have

‖η⁡(tT)​∫0tWRα,β​(t−τ)​g​𝑑τ‖Xs,12,σα,β\displaystyle\left\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)\int^{t}_{0}W_{R}^{\alpha,\beta}(t-\tau)g\,d\tau\right\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\frac{1}{2},\sigma}} ≤C​‖g‖Xs,σ−1α,β=C​‖η⁡(t2​T)​F‖Xs,σ−1α,β.\displaystyle\leq C\|g\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}}=C\Big\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{2T}\Big)F\Big\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,\sigma-1}}.

∎

Now we have developed all the tools needed to justify Lemma 6.7.

Proof of Lemma 6.7.

Firstly, we choose ϵ0=ϵ0​(s1,s2,α)>0\epsilon_{0}=\epsilon_{0}(s_{1},s_{2},\alpha)>0 as that in Lemma A.4. Then for any σ∈(12,12+ϵ0]\sigma\in(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_{0}], we apply Lemma A.5, with s=s2s=s_{2} and F=(w1​w2)xF=(w_{1}w_{2})_{x}, to conclude that

‖η⁡(tT)​∫0tWRα,β​(t−τ)​(w1​w2)x‖Xs2,12,σα,β≤C​‖η⁡(t2​T)​(w1​w2)x‖Xs2,σ−1α,β.\left\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)\int^{t}_{0}W_{R}^{\alpha,\beta}(t-\tau)(w_{1}w_{2})_{x}\right\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\leq C\Big\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{2T}\Big)(w_{1}w_{2})_{x}\Big\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\sigma-1}}.

Then it follows from Lemma A.4 that

‖η⁡(t2​T)​(w1​w2)x‖Xs2,σ−1α,β≤C​Tϵ0​(‖w1‖Xs1,12,σα,β​‖w2‖Xs2,12,σ−α,−β+‖w1‖Xs2,12,σα,β​‖w2‖Xs1,12,σ−α,−β),\Big\|\eta\Big(\frac{t}{2T}\Big)(w_{1}w_{2})_{x}\Big\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\sigma-1}}\leq CT^{\epsilon_{0}}\Big(\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{1},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}+\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s_{2},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{-\alpha,-\beta}_{s_{1},\frac{1}{2},\sigma}}\Big),

where C=C⁡(s1,s2,α,σ)C=C(s_{1},s_{2},\alpha,\sigma). Combining the above two estimates leads to (6.9) in Lemma 6.7. ∎
